title: T20's Arms Race: Fearless Batters, and Bowlers Learning to Think a Step Ahead
excerpt: An ESPNcricinfo analysis of the India-New Zealand series argues the format is mutating ball by ball — batters have abandoned fear, and bowlers are answering with deception and a new way of judging themselves. R Ashwin is not convinced India's attack is keeping up.
body:
• ESPNcricinfo's analysis of the India-New Zealand T20I series argues batters have shed fear entirely — front-foot shots are now step hits, good-length balls are slot balls, and right-handers switch-hit bowling plans into the bin.
  • Bowlers are evolving more slowly, the essay says, but they are evolving: Blair Tickner's knuckle ball and Arshdeep Singh's wobble seam show deception replacing stock pace, and bowlers now judge themselves on the quality of their thinking, not the outcome.
  • The series produced 2,030 runs across five matches, with Glenn Phillips' 341 the most ever by a batter in a bilateral series — yet India still won 3-2.
  • The counterpoint came from R Ashwin, who warned India's bowling — which conceded close to 200 or more three times — is a planning problem that will grow if not addressed.

T20 cricket is being pulled apart and rebuilt as a different game, and the five-match series between New Zealand and India — which India won 3-2 — offered the clearest recent evidence of how. That is the argument Alagappan Muthu makes in an ESPNcricinfo analysis published on November 1, tracing a running dialogue between bat and ball in which neither side holds the advantage for long.

Batters without fear

The essay opens with Mitchell Santner diving in vain as an Ishan Kishan drive missed him and was stopped only by the stumps at the non-striker's end — and Santner applauding the shot. From there, Muthu describes a format in which the old categories no longer hold. Front-foot shots are step hits now because they go for boundaries. Good-length balls are slot balls now because they are going for boundaries. A bowling plan built for a right-hander ends up in the bin because he decides to face it left-handed. In times gone by, he writes, the fear of what might go wrong kept shots and balls and stances in their traditional places. Now there is no fear.

The numbers from the series support the scale of the shift. A little dew and several oddly shaped New Zealand grounds helped, but the output was record-breaking: Glenn Phillips, the batter who bats with both hands, scored 341 runs, the most ever in a bilateral series, and the two teams combined for 2,030 runs. Only one other series between Full Member opposition has been as productive, the essay notes, and it helped that this one ran to five matches. Kishan's own adaptation is held up as the emblem of the new batting: denied a boundary by the stumps, he later met a similar delivery by opening his hips, closing the bat face and hitting a helicopter shot for four.

The bowlers' slower, quieter evolution

The piece does not argue that bowlers have been left behind entirely — it argues their progress is slower and judged differently. Early wickets still change games: Adam Milne removed both Sanju Samson and Abhishek Sharma in one match, leaving India's openers without a single boundary between them, a rarity that had happened just once since India became back-to-back T20 world champions, and giving New Zealand's quicks a longer spell with a swinging ball. Bounce, Muthu argues, is the great leveller: it is how New Zealand came back from conceding 90 runs in six overs, and also why India could score 90 in six overs after being 19 for 2 in 19 balls.

The clearest symbol is Blair Tickner's knuckle ball — delivered with a remarkably upright seam so it moves in the air, used to dismiss Naman Dhir, and celebrated by pulling a Pokemon card from his pocket. The knuckle ball, the essay says, is the bowler's switch hit: both involve changing the grip, both are means of deception, and both are really complicated. Arshdeep Singh, going wobble-seam across the right-hander, is offered as further proof that bowlers are not as far off the boil as feared. Perhaps the deepest change is mental: a bowler can produce his best ball and still be hit, so bowlers have learned to mark themselves on whether their thinking going into the delivery was right.

The counterpoint: planning, not just evolution

Not everyone left the series reassured. R Ashwin, speaking on his programme Ash ki Baat, criticised India's bowling through the series — close to 200 or more conceded three times — and questioned the planning behind a largely new-look attack missing Jasprit Bumrah. "What planning do they have? What are the talks in the meetings? If you don't address this, it will keep getting bigger," Ashwin said, calling the errors basic and the planning and execution very average. He also put the 3-2 scoreline in context: India chased 225 in the first match and recovered from 70 for 5 in the second, and New Zealand dropped 16 catches in the series. "We could have actually lost 4-1," he said.

Read together, the two accounts describe the same arms race from opposite ends. The analysis sees a format mutating ball by ball, where staying one step ahead — a grip change, a stance switch, a thought process recalibrated — is the whole game. Ashwin's warning is what happens to the side whose bowlers stop keeping pace. The contest moves to one-day cricket next: the ODI series begins on Wednesday, November 4, in Auckland.
